title: Ohms and Milliohms: Cable Resistance and Voltage Drop
h1: Ohms and milliohms — cable resistance, voltage drop, wire gauge
description: A 100 A load through 20 m of 6 mm² copper drops nearly 6 volts. Here is the resistance math behind wire sizing.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NEC Chapter 9 Table 8 and IEC 60228

hero: Copper is 17 milliohm-mm per metre. That single number, plus a cross-section, tells you every voltage drop calculation in a house or vehicle.
body: Wire resistance is often ignored — until it isn't. Undersized battery cables ruin cranking amps. Undersized branch circuits waste real power in heat. The math is straightforward once you have the resistivity constant.

> Copper resistivity ρ = 1.68 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m at 20°C
> Aluminium ρ = 2.65 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m (about 60% more resistive than copper)
> R = ρ × L / A
> 1 Ω = 1,000 mΩ = 10⁶ µΩ
> Rule of thumb: copper wire 1 mm² × 1 m ≈ 17.2 mΩ

AWG (American Wire Gauge) is a logarithmic scale — each 3 gauges halves the cross-sectional area. 10 AWG = 5.26 mm². 6 AWG = 13.3 mm². 2 AWG = 33.6 mm². Metric wire is sized directly in mm² of cross-section. Convert: mm² = 0.5067 × (92 / (36 / AWG − 2)) — or just use a table.

NEC recommends branch circuit voltage drop ≤3% at rated load, feeder ≤5%. A 20 A 120 V circuit dropping 3% (3.6 V) can lose up to 72 W just heating the wire — a full LED bulb per outlet in wasted energy. Longer runs need larger wire.
## Worked example — a 100 A load, 20 m of 6 mm² copper

R = 1.68 × 10⁻⁸ × 20 / (6 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.056 Ω per conductor. Round trip = 0.112 Ω. Voltage drop = 100 × 0.112 = 11.2 V. On a 230 V circuit: 4.9% drop — over the NEC limit. Upgrade to 10 mm² gives 6.72 V drop (2.9%). Power lost as heat in the 10 mm² cable: 672 W continuously.

A car starter draws 200–400 A briefly. A 30 mΩ cable (typical for a corroded connection) drops 6–12 V during cranking — enough to prevent starting on cold days. This is why 'clean your battery terminals' is the first suggestion for hard-start problems.
Copper: ~17 mΩ per m per mm². R = ρL/A. Voltage drop = I × R. Aim for ≤3% on branch circuits, ≤5% on feeders.

faqs.q: Is aluminium wire OK for house wiring?
faqs.a: Yes, at larger cross-sections. Aluminium has ~60% higher resistance than copper for the same area but is 50% cheaper. Common for service entries, less common for branch circuits due to termination oxidation issues.

faqs.q: How much does resistance change with temperature?
faqs.a: Copper: +0.393%/°C. A 20°C rise increases resistance by 8%. Hot cables get progressively hotter — a runaway path if oversizing was marginal.
A few pilot projects (Essen, LIPA on Long Island). Cost and cryogenics keep them niche. Conventional aluminium ACSR still dominates power transmission.
